segments.say: So far, we've mostly talked about speeches and essays. But some of the things people put off matter even more. Booking a check-up. Calling about a pain that won't go away. Starting the gentle exercise a doctor suggested. These tasks often carry exactly the feelings that make us delay. Worry, uncertainty, and the fear of hearing something we'd rather not hear.

show.title: The things we put off most

segments.say: In 2003, Fuschia Sirois, Michelle Melia-Gordon and Timothy Pychyl published a study with a title many people will recognize. I'll look after my health, later. They found that people who procrastinated more tended to report more stress and to carry out fewer everyday health habits, the small routines of looking after ourselves. Later work by Sirois built this into what she called a procrastination and health model.

show.who: Fuschia Sirois, Michelle Melia-Gordon and Timothy Pychyl
show.what: Procrastination, stress and looking after our health

segments.say: The idea is that procrastination may affect health along two paths. One path runs through stress, the worry and pressure that pile up when things are left undone. The other runs through behaviour, the check-ups not booked, the walks not taken, the early nights postponed. Neither path is dramatic on any single day. But over months and years, small delays can quietly add up.

So if there's one area where a small, kind step is especially worth taking, it might be this one. The kindest delays to stop are often the ones about our own health. A phone call that takes three minutes can lift a worry that has been sitting in the background for weeks. And it's usually much less frightening than the waiting was.

show.text: The kindest delays to stop are the ones about our health.

segments.say: But let's end this part of our investigation on a lighter note, with a philosopher who decided to work with his procrastination rather than against it. John Perry, a philosopher at Stanford University, wrote a short, playful essay in the 1990s called Structured Procrastination. Years later, the idea won him an Ig Nobel Prize, the light-hearted award for research that first makes people laugh, and then makes them think.

Perry noticed something about himself. Procrastinators rarely do nothing. They do lots of things, just not the thing at the top of the list. So his idea was to use that tendency on purpose. Put a big, important-looking task at the top of your list, and you'll find yourself happily doing all the useful smaller tasks below it, as a way of avoiding the big one.

It's a funny idea, and Perry presented it with a wink. A big task at the top of the list. Useful tasks below it. And then you avoid the top one by doing all the rest. Ben's spice rack is, in a way, a small example. It got done beautifully, precisely because the speech was hovering above it.

show.title: Structured procrastination
items: A big task at the top
Avoid the top by doing the rest

segments.say: Of course, structured procrastination has its limits. It works best when the task at the top isn't really urgent, and when the tasks below are genuinely useful. It doesn't help much when the top task is a wedding speech due on Saturday. But it carries a kind and useful message. Procrastinators aren't broken. They're often full of energy, just pointed in a slightly unexpected direction.

And that's a hopeful place to arrive. If the energy is already there, then the question isn't how to become a different person. It's how to gently point that energy at what matters most. How to make the important task feel a little smaller, a little nicer, and a little nearer. And that's exactly what we'll look at now, with a handful of small, practical ideas.

Perry's essay is a reminder that most procrastinators aren't short of effort. Ben spent a whole Sunday evening being very busy. What he lacked wasn't energy, and it wasn't care. It was a way of making the first step toward the speech feel as easy as the first step toward the spice rack. And that, it turns out, is something we can work on.
